echoes.note: The vineyard (ampelon) is the master's estate where laborers are hired; Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard establishes the vineyard as Israel/God's people under his care and reckoning. Matthew reuses this stock symbol (cf. the next parable, 21:33-41, which quotes Isa 5 directly), framing the kingdom under the imagery of God's vineyard.
The vine/vineyard brought out of Egypt and tended by God is part of the same symbolic field; faint thematic resonance behind the kingdom-as-vineyard image rather than verbal borrowing.

The Torah commands paying a hired laborer his wages the same day, before sundown: 'When evening had come... pay them their wages' (20:8) directly enacts this hired-laborer wage law, giving the parable its legal verisimilitude and its concern with what is 'right' (dikaion).
Parallel wage-law ('the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning'); reinforces the same-day payment background of 20:8.

'Is your eye evil because I am good?' (20:15) uses the Semitic idiom of the 'evil eye' (ophthalmos ponēros) for grudging stinginess; Deut 15:9 warns against the eye being 'evil' (begrudging) toward a needy brother — the exact moral idiom Jesus inverts (here it is the workers who begrudge the master's generosity).
'Do not eat the bread of him who has an evil eye' — same 'evil eye'=miserly idiom standing behind 20:15; faint, idiomatic rather than allusive.

'It is my desire to give... Isn't it lawful for me to do what I want with what I own?' (20:14-15) echoes God's sovereign freedom in mercy ('I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious'); thematic, disputed.
'The burden of the day and the scorching heat' (20:12) faintly recalls the scorching east wind/heat motif; very weak, likely just realistic detail of agricultural labor.

The Son of Man 'will be delivered/handed over' (paradothēsetai) to the authorities and Gentiles; paradidōmi is the verb the Greek of Isaiah 53 uses for the Servant being 'handed over' for sins (Isa 53:6,12 LXX), coloring the passion prediction with Servant theology.
'to mock, to scourge' (20:19) corresponds to the Servant who gives his back to those who strike and his face to mocking/spitting; the catalog of mistreatment draws on the third Servant Song.

'the third day he will be raised up' (20:19) echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him'; widely read as the scriptural background for the 'third day' resurrection formula.
'the Son of Man' (20:18) carries the Danielic title; here paradoxically the exalted Danielic figure is the one delivered up to death, a Matthean recurrence of the title.

'the cup that I am about to drink' (20:22) is the prophetic 'cup of wrath/staggering' that Jerusalem drinks (Isa 51:17,22); Jesus takes upon himself the cup of judgment, the dominant OT background for the passion-cup.
The cup of foaming wine of God's wrath that the wicked drink to the dregs; supplies the 'cup' = divine judgment imagery behind 20:22-23.
'Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and make all the nations drink it' — the cup of wrath passed to the nations; reinforces the cup-of-judgment field Jesus says he must drink.
The cup of horror and desolation that Jerusalem must drink to the dregs; same cup-of-wrath motif, fainter parallel.
The request to sit at Jesus' right hand and left in his kingdom faintly invokes enthronement-at-the-right-hand language; weak, the verbal contact is only 'right hand.'

The 'baptism' of overwhelming suffering pairs with the cup; the engulfing-waters imagery of the righteous sufferer ('the waters have come up to my neck') is a faint background for being 'baptized' with suffering.

KEY allusion. 'The Son of Man came... to give his life as a ransom for many' (20:28) compresses the fourth Servant Song: the Servant 'pours out his soul to death' and 'bears the sin of many' (Isa 53:12), making his life an offering (asham, 53:10). 'Give his life' (dounai tēn psychēn) + 'for many' (anti pollōn) maps onto the LXX Servant who is handed over for the 'many' (polloi, Isa 53:11-12). Vicarious, substitutionary death — the figural fulfillment of the Servant.

Jesus identifies himself as the one who came 'to serve' (diakonēsai); the title 'Son of Man' is overlaid on the exalted 'my Servant' (pais) of Isaiah, framing his whole mission as the Servant of YHWH who suffers and is exalted.

'The rulers of the nations lord it over them... it shall not be so among you' (20:25-26) inverts the false shepherds of Israel who 'with force and harshness ruled them'; Jesus contrasts domineering rule with self-giving service in the shepherd-leadership idiom of Ezek 34.
Rehoboam's choice to make his yoke heavier and rule harshly over against serving the people is a narrative type of lordly domination Jesus repudiates; thematic, disputed.

God 'gave Egypt as your ransom (LXX allagma/lytron), Cush and Seba in exchange for you... I give people in return for your life'; supplies the ransom-in-exchange-for-life logic of lytron anti pollōn in 20:28.
Each Israelite gives a 'ransom (lytra) for his life' at the census so that no plague falls; background to the ransom-price (lytron) vocabulary, though Jesus' self-gift transcends the cultic fee.

'No man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him, for the redemption of their life is costly'; Jesus' ransom answers the impossibility the psalm laments — faint, ironic counterpoint.

'the Son of Man' (20:28) again carries the Danielic title; the one given dominion and service by the nations is here the one who himself comes to serve, a deliberate Matthean inversion of the Danielic enthronement.

'that our eyes may be opened... their eyes received their sight' (20:33-34) enacts the messianic-age promise 'then the eyes of the blind shall be opened'; the healing functions as a sign that the awaited deliverance has arrived (cf. Matt 11:5).
The Servant is called 'to open the eyes that are blind'; the blind men's healing realizes the Servant's commission — tying this episode back to the Servant theme just sounded in 20:28.
'Son of David, have mercy on us!' (20:30-31) invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's seed; the blind confess Jesus as the messianic Son of David.
The 'shoot from the stump of Jesse' stands behind the Son-of-David / Davidic-messiah confession; thematic support for the title in 20:30.
'the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' — additional eschatological sight-restoration promise reinforcing the Isaianic background of the healing.
'Have mercy on us (eleēson hēmas), O LORD, have mercy on us' — the doubled cry of the blind (20:30-31) reuses the stock psalmic plea for mercy; idiomatic rather than a specific citation.
